What is sqtseries?

Abbreviations used on this page (TSDB, WAL, TTL, HWM, XPUB, ZMQ, SQLite, JSON, CLI, API, RSS, fd, PEP, CORS, OBS...) are defined in the Abbreviations & jargon section.

sqtseries is a program that lets you record measurements — temperature, CPU usage, website visits, stock prices, energy use, anything that changes over time — and later ask questions like "what was the average this last hour?", "what is the latest reading?", or "how did it change day by day?". The answers come back in milliseconds, and stay fast even after you have stored millions of numbers.

It is designed for your own projects rather than big shared services. You do not install a separate database server: sqtseries run starts the service, its data lives in a single SQLite file on your machine (~/.sqtseries/data/db.sqlite by default), and you can copy, back up, or delete that file like any other. It also ships a ZeroMQ message bus and an HTTP gateway, so programs written in other languages can send it data and read results too.

Behind the scenes, the engine keeps your questions fast without you doing anything: measurements are stored in monthly partitions, and a background task pre-aggregates every completed hour into a summary table. A query about months of history reads a handful of summary rows instead of every stored point, so wide queries stay fast as the data grows.

One file database

Everything lives in one SQLite file in WAL mode, split into monthly partitions. Consistent backups are one command away.

Fast, crash-safe writes

Every measurement is written in its own transaction the moment it arrives — no batch buffer to lose or flush. SQLite's WAL journal makes every write atomic.

Fast reads

Queries draw on a built-in hourly summary table, so a question about months of data reads a handful of rows instead of every stored point.

Two ways to talk

ZeroMQ (a message bus) and HTTP (web requests). The bundled Python client (sqtseries.Client) talks ZeroMQ; plain HTTP works from any tool.

Try it

Install sqtseries and start the service, then send and read back some data. The whole loop is a few commands:

pip install sqtseries
sqtseries run

In another terminal, send a measurement and read it back:

from sqtseries import Client

c = Client()
c.write("cpu.usage", 0.72, {"host": "web1"})

rows = c.query("cpu.usage", aggregation="avg", interval="1m")
print(rows)

You can also use plain HTTP from any tool that speaks it:

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/write \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"metric":"cpu.usage","value":0.72}'
curl "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/read?metric=cpu.usage&limit=5"

Camera analytics

A camera with edge analytics streams JSON over a WebSocket — people and vehicle counts, battery and CPU telemetry, every quarter second. sqtseries stores each number as a flat measurement tagged with the camera ID, and then answers the questions that matter: busiest hour, footfall trend, battery drain rate and time-to-empty, CPU/thermal profile, feed uptime, and more.

The repo ships a self-contained demo: camera/overlay_server.py simulates the camera feed on a random port and serves a live dashboard page, camera/camera_feed.py pumps it into sqtseries over plain HTTP (no sqtseries installed needed — just websockets), and camera/camera_feed.py --ask answers 17 questions from the stored data. One command — examples/camera/sqtcam.sh — starts sqtseries, the simulator, and the feed in a tmux session so you can leave it collecting data overnight. See Camera analytics for the full walkthrough.

Ports

The service is configured to listen on these six local ports (defaults; note the ingest port is auto-detected from 12500 when ports.auto_detect is on, so it is usually 12500, not 12501):

PortPurposeProtocolDoc
12501IngestionZMQ PULLIngestion
12502QueriesZMQ REPQueries
12503Live streamingZMQ XPUBStreaming
12504Admin commandsZMQ REPAdmin
12505HTTP gatewayHTTP + WebSocketHTTP API
12506Stats eventsZMQ PUBAdmin

All sockets are local only (bound to 127.0.0.1). Of the six, only the ingest port is auto-detected: run scans the port range (default 12500–12700, plus ports.port_offset) for the first free port, skipping the query/streaming/admin/http/stats ports it is told to avoid (ports.auto_detect). The other five ports are fixed — if one of them is already bound, startup fails so you can fix the conflict. The active ports are shown by sqtseries ports and stored in runtime.json next to the database.
